claim: In albino mice and EphB1 knockout mice, mistargeted retinal ganglion cell axons form dense islands of axon terminals in the dorsal lateral geniculate nuclei (dLGN).
source: In albino mice and EphB1 knockout mice, mistargeted retinal ganglion cell axons form dense islands of axon terminals in the dorsal lateral geniculate nuclei (dLGN).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Rebsam et al., 2012; Rebsam et al., 2009) and by data presented in the manuscript showing CtB labeling of islands in albino mice.

claim: The formation of these islands of retinal input depends on developmental patterns of spontaneous retinal activity.
source: The formation of these islands of retinal input depends on developmental patterns of spontaneous retinal activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies showing that blocking retinal waves prevents island formation (Rebsam et al., 2009; Rebsam et al., 2012).

claim: The boundaries of the island represent a remarkably strong segregation within retinogeniculate connectivity.
source: We reconstructed the microcircuitry of the activity-dependent islands and found that the boundaries of the island represent a remarkably strong segregation within retinogeniculate connectivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by EM reconstruction data showing that TCs are innervated exclusively by either island or non-island RGC boutons.

claim: When sets of retinal input are established in the wrong part of the dLGN, the developing circuitry responds by forming a synaptically isolated subcircuit within the otherwise fully connected network.
source: We conclude that when sets of retinal input are established in the wrong part of the dLGN, the developing circuitry responds by forming a synaptically isolated subcircuit within the otherwise fully connected network.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the EM reconstruction data showing complete segregation of island and non-island connectivity to TCs.

claim: Activity-dependent synaptic remodeling is a process in which patterns of neuron depolarization and synaptic transmission determine whether a given synapse will be maintained, enhanced, or eliminated.
source: Activity-dependent synaptic remodeling is a process in which patterns of neuron depolarization and synaptic transmission determine whether a given synapse will be maintained, enhanced, or eliminated (Katz and Shatz, 1996; Lichtman and Colman, 2000; Redfern, 1970; Lichtman, 1977; Crepel et al., 1976).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature on activity-dependent synaptic remodeling.

claim: The dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (dLGN) provides the most direct link between the retina and visual cortex in amniotes.
source: In amniotes (birds, reptiles, mammals), the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (dLGN) provides the most direct link between the retina and visual cortex.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the visual system anatomy in amniotes.

claim: The dLGN's functional architecture is similar to that of the inner plexiform layer of the retina, with both consisting of multiple topographic maps of visual space stacked together as functionally distinct layers.
source: The dLGN's functional architecture is similar to that of their immediate upstream circuit, the inner plexiform layer of the retina. Both neuropils consist of multiple topographic maps of visual space stacked together as functionally distinct layers (Reese, 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Reese, 1988.

claim: The functional architecture of the dLGN depends heavily on an extended period of activity-dependent synaptic remodeling.
source: Unlike the architecture of the retina, the functional architecture of the dLGN depends heavily on an extended period of activity-dependent synaptic remodeling (Chen and Regehr, 2000; Stellwagen and Shatz, 2002; Lee et al., 2002; Godement et al., 1984; Hahm et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on dLGN development.

claim: Blocking the spontaneous waves of activity disrupts the refinement of dLGN retinotopy.
source: Blocking the spontaneous waves of activity disrupts the refinement of dLGN retinotopy (Grubb et al., 2003; Pfeiffenberger et al., 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Blocking spontaneous waves of activity disrupts the normal segregation of left and right eye inputs in the dLGN.
source: Blocking the spontaneous waves of activity disrupts...the normal segregation of left and right eye inputs (Feller, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Feller, 2009.

claim: The innervation of the dLGN by the retina starts with molecular gradients guiding axons to roughly the correct location.
source: The innervation of the dLGN by the retina starts with molecular gradients guiding axons to roughly the correct location (Sitko et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sitko et al., 2018.

claim: RGC axons form synapses with many more thalamocortical cells (TCs) than they will innervate in the adult.
source: where they form synapses with many more thalamocortical cells (TCs) than they will innervate in the adult (Chen and Regehr, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chen and Regehr, 2000.

claim: The retina generates spontaneous waves of activity in which retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) with similar positions and receptive field properties fire together.
source: The retina then generates spontaneous waves of activity in which retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) with similar positions and receptive field properties fire together (Meister et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Meister et al., 1991.

claim: The temporal correlation of RGC firing is thought to help refine the innervation of the dLGN according to Hebbian rules.
source: The temporal correlation of this RGC firing is thought to help refine the innervation of the dLGN according to Hebbian rules (Butts et al., 2007; Lee et al., 2002; Morris and Hebb, 1949).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and represents a theoretical framework.

claim: By selecting a set of RGC inputs that fire at the same time, TCs can ensure that their inputs are driven by a single region of space and have similar functional properties.
source: By selecting a set of RGC inputs that fire at the same time, TCs can ensure that their inputs are driven by a single region of space and have similar functional properties.
evidence: This is an inference based on Hebbian theory and the known properties of retinal waves.

claim: The result of activity-dependent refinement is a refined map of visual space where nearby TCs share functional properties and, often, RGC inputs.
source: The result is a refined map of visual space where nearby TC share functional properties and, often, RGC inputs (Morgan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Morgan et al., 2016.

claim: In albino mice (B6(Cg)-Tyrc-2J/J) and EphB1-knockout mice, sets of RGC axons that would normally project to the ipsilateral dLGN instead project to the contralateral dLGN.
source: In albino mice (B6(Cg)-Tyrc-2J/J) (Rebsam et al., 2012) and EphB1-knockout mice (Rebsam et al., 2009), sets of RGC axons that would normally project to the ipsilateral dLGN instead project to the contralateral dLGN.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rebsam et al., 2012 and Rebsam et al., 2009.

claim: Some of the mistargeted axons in albino and EphB1-knockout mice form islands of intense bouton labeling within the dLGN.
source: Some of these mistargeted axons form islands of intense bouton labeling within the dLGN.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Blocking developmental retinal waves prevents the formation of these islands.
source: Blocking developmental retinal waves prevents the formation of these islands (Rebsam et al., 2009; Rebsam et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: RGC axons in the island form the complex retinogeniculate synaptic glomeruli typical of normal dLGN.
source: We find that RGC axons in the island form the complex retinogeniculate synaptic glomeruli typical of normal dLGN.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The island reflects a segregated microcircuit where mistargeted axons capture an exclusive set of TCs.
source: We found that the island does, in fact, reflect a segregated microcircuit where mistargeted axons capture an exclusive set of TCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by EM reconstruction data showing exclusive connectivity patterns.

claim: The dLGNs of all 12 albino mice examined showed bright, distinct islands of contralaterally projecting RGC boutons.
source: Consistent with previous studies, we found that the dLGNs of all 12 mice examined showed bright, distinct islands of contralaterally projecting RGC boutons (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from 12 mice and reference to Figure 1.

claim: CtB labeling of RGC boutons within the island resembled labeling of RGC boutons outside of the island with the exception that the density of labeling was higher within the island.
source: Confocal imaging of the CTB-labeled albino dLGNs showed that CtB labeling of RGC boutons within the island resembled labeling of RGC boutons outside of the island with the exception that the density of labeling was higher within the island (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Both inside and outside of the island, the fluorescent profile of bright dots surrounding a dark spot is consistent with synaptic glomeruli in which labeled RGC boutons clustered around unlabeled TC dendrites.
source: Both inside and outside of the island, we observed the fluorescent profile of bright dots surrounding a dark spot. This profile is consistent with synaptic glomeruli in which labeled RGC boutons clustered around unlabeled TC dendrites (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is based on interpretation of confocal imaging data and comparison to known glomerular structure.

claim: The island was surrounded by an RGC-bouton-free region, termed the exclusion zone.
source: Confocal imaging also made it clear that the island was surrounded by an RGC-bouton-free region, which we term the exclusion zone.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging data.

claim: The exclusion zone was composed of a mix of neuropil, cell nuclei, myelinated fibers, and an occasional blood vessel.
source: Examination of this exclusion zone with autofluorescence, reflected light, and immunolabeling for synaptophysin (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) demonstrates that the exclusion zone was composed of a mix of neuropil, cell nuclei, myelinated fibers, and an occasional blood vessel.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple imaging modalities and reference to figures.

claim: No anatomical barrier was detected that would preclude RGC boutons from forming in the exclusion zone region.
source: We did not detect an anatomical barrier that would preclude RGC boutons from forming in this region.
evidence: This is a negative finding based on examination of the exclusion zone.

claim: RGC boutons in the island participated in normal retinogeniculate synaptic glomeruli.
source: We found that RGC boutons in the island participated in normal retinogeniculate synaptic glomeruli (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlated light and electron microscopy data.

claim: RGC boutons were identified by their light mitochondria, large size, and large synaptic vesicles.
source: RGC boutons were identified by their light mitochondria, large size, and large synaptic vesicles (Hamos et al., 1987).
evidence: This claim is based on established ultrastructural criteria cited from Hamos et al., 1987.

claim: Thalamocortical dendrites were distinguished from local inhibitory neuron dendrites by the presence of spines and the absence of synaptic outputs.
source: Thalamocortical dendrites were distinguished from local inhibitory neuron dendrites by the presence of spines and the absence of synaptic outputs.
evidence: This is based on established ultrastructural criteria for identifying cell types.

claim: RGC boutons form normal synaptic triads innervating local inhibitory neuron boutons that then form inhibitory synapses onto TCs.
source: The RGC boutons form normal synaptic triads innervating local inhibitory neuron boutons that then form inhibitory synapses onto TCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by EM data showing the synaptic organization.

claim: The cluster of RGC and local inhibitory neuron boutons are encapsulated by a glial sheath.
source: As in normal dLGN, the cluster of RGC and local inhibitory neuron boutons are encapsulated by a glial sheath (Saavedra and Vaccarezza, 1968).
evidence: This claim is supported by EM data and citation to Saavedra and Vaccarezza, 1968.

claim: Electron microscopy of the exclusion zone revealed large regions of dLGN neuropil with no RGC boutons.
source: Consistent with the CtB labeling, electron microscopy (EM) of the exclusion zone revealed large regions of dLGN neuropil with no RGC boutons (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by EM data and reference to Figure 1D.

claim: Aside from the lack of RGC glomeruli, the exclusion zone appeared healthy.
source: Aside from the lack of RGC glomeruli, the exclusion zone appeared healthy.
evidence: This is an assessment based on EM examination of the tissue.

claim: The synaptic neuropil of the exclusion zone was composed of non-glomerular synapses and their associated neurites.
source: The synaptic neuropil of the exclusion zone was composed of non-glomerular synapses and their associated neurites (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by EM data and reference to Figure 1D.

claim: The bright islands of CtB labeling observed in the albino dLGN represent a high concentration of ultrastructurally normal RGC boutons embedded in healthy dLGN neuropil.
source: Our examination of RGC boutons in the dLGN of the albino mouse, therefore, rules out the possibility that the islands are dead-end neuromas buried in the optic tract. Rather, the bright islands of CtB labeling observed in the albino dLGN represent a high concentration of ultrastructurally normal RGC boutons embedded in healthy dLGN neuropil.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the combined optical and EM data presented.

claim: The pattern of RGC innervation of TCs defines the functional architecture of the dLGN.
source: TCs are the sole output neuron of the dLGN, and their receptive field properties are largely the product of which RGCs innervate them (Usrey et al., 1998). The pattern of RGC innervation of TCs, therefore, defines the functional architecture of the dLGN.
evidence: This claim is based on citation and logical inference about dLGN function.

claim: In previous EM reconstructions of mouse dLGN circuitry, nearby TCs tend to be innervated by the same RGC axons.
source: In previous EM reconstructions of mouse dLGN circuitry, we found that nearby TCs tend to be innervated by the same RGC axons (Morgan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Morgan et al., 2016.

claim: If the exclusion zone represents a segregation of retinogeniculate circuitry, TCs near the exclusion zone would be innervated by either the island or non-island RGC boutons, not both.
source: By contrast, If the exclusion zone around the RGC island represents a segregation of retinogeniculate circuitry, we would expect to find a hard boundary in connectivity. TCs near the exclusion zone would be innervated by either the island or non-island RGC boutons, not both.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the Hebbian model of activity-dependent development.

claim: A serial section EM volume was collected consisting of 2631 40-nm-thick coronal sections.
source: The EM volume was obtained from an optically characterized albino dLGN and consisted of 2631 40-nm-thick coronal sections (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods and data collection.

claim: From each section, a 220 μm × 220 μm image mosaic was acquired that encompassed most of the albino island, the exclusion zone, and the surrounding non-island dLGN neuropil (105 μm of rostro-caudal z-depth).
source: From each section, we acquired a 220 μm × 220 μm image mosaic that encompassed most of the albino island, the exclusion zone, and the surrounding non-island dLGN neuropil (105 μm of rostro-caudal z-depth).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods and data collection.

claim: Images were acquired with a 20 nm pixel size.
source: Images were acquired with a 20 nm pixel size.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: 15 TCs whose nuclei were distributed across the RGC island exclusion zone were traced.
source: We traced 15 TCs whose nuclei were distributed across the RGC island exclusion zone (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental analysis performed.

claim: 14 TCs were innervated either exclusively by the island (six TCs) or exclusively by RGC boutons outside of the island (eight TCs).
source: We found that 14 TCs were innervated either exclusively by the island (six TCs) or exclusively by RGC boutons outside of the island (eight TCs, Figure 2F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by EM reconstruction data and reference to figures.

claim: There were no mixed non-island/island TCs.
source: There were no mixed non-island/island TCs.
evidence: This is a key finding from the EM reconstruction data.

claim: There was one TC that received inputs in the exclusion zone and one TC on which no RGC inputs could be found.
source: There was one TC (mentioned above) that received inputs in the exclusion zone and one TC on which no RGC inputs could be found.
evidence: This is a description of exceptions found in the EM reconstruction data.

claim: The wide range of the number of RGC boutons innervating TCs (0–118) may reflect the fact that, in the dorsal mouse dLGN, synaptic inputs from the superior colliculus can take the place of RGCs as a primary driving synapse.
source: The wide range of the number of RGC boutons innervating TCs (0–118, Figure 2G) may reflect the fact that, in the dorsal mouse dLGN, synaptic inputs from the superior colliculus can take the place of RGCs as a primary driving synapse (Bickford et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data based on citation to Bickford et al., 2015.

claim: 99% of the Monte Carlo iterations produced four (44%) or fewer captured TCs.
source: We found that 99% of the Monte Carlo iterations produced four (44%) or fewer captured TCs (Figure 2I).
evidence: This claim is supported by Monte Carlo simulation results.

claim: The nine captured TCs (100%) represent a substantial deviation from an unbiased assignment of dendrites to island or non-island RGCs.
source: The nine captured TCs (100%), therefore, represent a substantial deviation from an unbiased assignment of dendrites to island or non-island RGCs.
evidence: This conclusion is based on comparison of observed data to Monte Carlo simulation results.

claim: The absence of TCs that were innervated both by the island and non-island RGC boutons means that the island represents a segregation of retinogeniculate synaptic connectivity.
source: The absence of TCs that were innervated both by the island and non-island RGC boutons means that the island represents a segregation of retinogeniculate synaptic connectivity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the EM reconstruction data.

claim: The asymmetry of TC dendritic arbors was clearly oriented away from the exclusion zone.
source: What was noteworthy was that the asymmetry was so clearly oriented away from the exclusion zone.
evidence: This is an observation from the EM reconstruction data.

claim: Few TC dendrites crossed into the exclusion zone and those that did assumed a distal dendrite morphology.
source: Few TC dendrites crossed into the exclusion zone and those that did assumed a distal dendrite morphology (Figure 2H and J, Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and2, Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by EM reconstruction data and reference to figures.

claim: The presence of cortical feedback synapses on the dendrites that span the exclusion zone means that the cortical feedback onto the TCs does not obey the strict island/non-island segregation exhibited by the RGC innervation.
source: The presence of cortical feedback synapses (small round boutons innervating small spines, Guillery, 1971) on the dendrites that span the exclusion zone means that the cortical feedback onto the TCs does not obey the strict island/non-island segregation exhibited by the RGC innervation.
evidence: This conclusion is based on EM data showing cortical feedback synapses in the exclusion zone.

claim: In mouse, RGC inputs to TCs are almost always coupled with connections to local inhibitory neurons (LINs).
source: In mouse, RGC inputs to TCs are almost always coupled with connections to local inhibitory neurons (LINs) (Morgan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Morgan et al., 2016.

claim: Local inhibitory neurons form three types of neurites: (1) input/output shaft dendrites that span hundreds of micrometers and multiple subregions of the dLGN, (2) input/output targeted dendrites that extend about 20 μm from the shaft dendrites and closely follow nearby RGC axons, and (3) output-only axons that are relatively small.
source: These inhibitory neurons form three types of neurites: (1) input/output shaft dendrites that span hundreds of micrometers and multiple subregions of the dLGN, (2) input/output targeted dendrites that extend about 20 μm from the shaft dendrites and closely follow nearby RGC axons, and (3) output-only axons that are relatively small (Morgan and Lichtman, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Morgan and Lichtman, 2020.

claim: The short distances between the output synapses of the targeted neurites and multiple RGC inputs mean the targeted neurites can provide a synaptic drive that reflects the functional properties of the local dLGN neuropil.
source: The short distances between the output synapses of the targeted neurites and multiple RGC inputs mean the targeted neurites can provide a synaptic drive that reflects the functional properties of the local dLGN neuropil (Morgan and Lichtman, 2020).
evidence: This claim is based on citation and inference about the functional properties of targeted neurites.

claim: Output synapses on the shaft dendrites of LINs are expected to be driven more by the global integration of inputs across the large LIN dendritic arbor.
source: Output synapses on the shaft dendrites of LINs, in contrast, are expected to be driven more by the global integration of inputs across the large LIN dendritic arbor.
evidence: This is an inference based on the morphology and connectivity of shaft dendrites.

claim: The shaft neurites of local inhibitory neurons would be indifferent to the boundaries of the RGC island while individually targeted neurites would be associated with either island or non-island RGC boutons.
source: Based on these properties, we hypothesized that the shaft neurites of local inhibitory neurons would be indifferent to the boundaries of the RGC island while individually targeted neurites would be associated with either island or non-island RGC boutons.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the known properties of LIN neurites.

claim: In GAD67-GFP transgenic mice, dLGN local inhibitory neurons are brightly labeled with GFP.
source: In GAD67-GFP transgenic mice, dLGN local inhibitory neurons are brightly labeled with GFP (Seabrook et al., 2013; Charalambakis et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies using GAD67-GFP mice.

claim: Airyscan confocal images of the island revealed LIN dendrites that were closely associated with the CtB labeling of RGC boutons.
source: Airyscan confocal images of the island revealed LIN dendrites that were closely associated with the CtB labeling of RGC boutons (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging data and reference to Figure 3B.

claim: The tight association with RGC boutons is characteristic of the targeted dendrites of LINs.
source: This tight association with RGC boutons is characteristic of the targeted dendrites of LINS.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of LIN morphology.

claim: The shaft dendrites of LINs crossed the RGC bouton exclusion zone without obvious deviation.
source: In contrast, the shaft dendrites of LINs crossed the RGC bouton exclusion zone without obvious deviation (Figure 3A and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging data and reference to figures.

claim: This pattern of LIN dendrite behavior was consistent across five mice examined.
source: This pattern was consistent across five mice examined.
evidence: This indicates reproducibility of the observation across multiple animals.

claim: One LIN extended dendrites into both the island and non-island neuropil and formed synapses with RGCs and TCs in both regions.
source: This LIN extended dendrites into both the island and non-island neuropil and formed synapses with RGCs and TCs in both regions (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by EM reconstruction data and reference to Figure 3D.

claim: Two LIN tracings revealed long targeted neurites that formed many connections to TCs and RGCs specifically within either the island or non-island neuropil.
source: Two of these tracings revealed long targeted neurites that formed many connections to TCs and RGCs specifically within either the island or non-island neuropil (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by EM reconstruction data and reference to Figure 3E.

claim: One LIN dendrite received 4 island boutons near its base and then received 42 synapses from non-island RGC boutons.
source: This dendrite was interesting in that it received 4 island boutons near its base and then received 42 synapses from non-island RGC boutons.
evidence: This is a specific observation from the EM reconstruction data.

claim: The LIN results are consistent with the prediction that shaft dendrites would be indifferent to island/non-island boundaries while individual targeted dendrites would target either the island or non-island RGC boutons.
source: The LIN results are consistent with our prediction that shaft dendrites would be indifferent to island/non-island boundaries while individual targeted dendrites would target either the island or non-island RGC boutons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison of the hypothesis to the observed data.

claim: The restriction of the targeted dendrites to one or the other RGC field does not appear to be an absolute rule.
source: However, the restriction of the targeted dendrites to one or the other RGC field does not appear to be an absolute rule.
evidence: This is a qualification based on the observation of one dendrite receiving inputs from both island and non-island RGCs.

claim: The scale of targeted dendrite exploration and the size of the exclusion zone are likely to reduce the chances that a targeted dendrite would find partners on both in the island and outside of the island.
source: Rather the scale of targeted dendrite exploration and the size of the exclusion zone are likely to reduce the chances that a targeted dendrite would find partners on both in the island and outside of the island.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial relationships observed in the data.

claim: This matching between the exploration of targeted LIN dendrites and the segregation of retinogeniculate connectivity means that targeted LIN dendrites will have an RGC input profile (island/non-island) that matches the TCs they innervate.
source: This matching between the exploration of targeted LIN dendrites and the segregation of retinogeniculate connectivity means that targeted LIN dendrites will have an RGC input profile (island/non-island) that matches the TCs they innervate.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observed connectivity patterns.

claim: The previously reported islands of mistargeted RGC terminals represent a segregation of retinogeniculate circuitry into distinct pathways.
source: The key conclusion of this study is that the previously reported islands of mistargeted RGC terminals represent a segregation of retinogeniculate circuitry into distinct pathways.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all the data presented.

claim: In a previous EM reconstruction of a wildtype mouse dLGN, nearby TCs shared input from the same RGC axons even when the RGC axons or TCs were of morphologically distinct types.
source: In a previous EM reconstruction of a wildtype mouse dLGN, nearby TCs shared input from the same RGC axons even when the RGC axons or TCs were of morphologically distinct types (Morgan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Morgan et al., 2016.

claim: The parallel pathways of different types of RGCs do not have synaptically clean boundaries in the mouse dLGN, but instead are frequently intermixed.
source: Based on these results, we argued that the parallel pathways of different types of RGCs did not have synaptically clean boundaries in the mouse dLGN, but instead were frequently intermixed.
evidence: This is a conclusion from previous work by the authors.

claim: The island/non-island projections appear truly parallel (non-intersecting).
source: In contrast, the island/non-island projections appear truly parallel (non-intersecting).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data showing no mixed connectivity.

claim: In cats and primates, the receptive field properties of TCs are usually derived from a strong innervation from a few functionally similar RGCs.
source: In cats and primates, the receptive field properties of TCs are usually derived from a strong innervation from a few functionally similar RGCs (Usrey et al., 1998; Mastronarde, 1992; Hamos et al., 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies in cats and primates.

claim: This connectivity allows for a spatially continuous sampling of visual space with little loss in acuity.
source: This connectivity allows for a spatially continuous sampling of visual space with little loss in acuity (Alonso et al., 2006; Martinez et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and represents an inference about visual processing.

claim: Mouse TCs can be innervated by dozens of RGCs.
source: Mouse TCs can be innervated by dozens of RGCs (Morgan et al., 2016; Hammer et al., 2015; Rompani et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies of mouse dLGN.

claim: Different RGC types innervate the same TC in mouse.
source: and different RGC types innervate the same TC (Liang et al., 2018; Marshel et al., 2012; Rompani et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies of mouse dLGN.

claim: The mouse dLGN contains both high- and low-convergence TCs.
source: Part of the explanation of the discrepancy is that the mouse dLGN contains both high- and low-convergence TCs (Morgan et al., 2016; Rompani et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies of mouse dLGN.

claim: Many of the RGC inputs to a given mouse TC are much weaker than the relatively few RGCs that dominate the TC firing.
source: Further, many of the RGC inputs to a given mouse TC are much weaker than the relatively few RGCs that dominate the TC firing (Litvina et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Litvina et al., 2017.

claim: Within the circuitry of the mouse dLGN, there are TCs whose connectivity is consistent with the gated relays of retinal activity described in other species.
source: Within the circuitry of the mouse dLGN, therefore, there are TCs whose connectivity is consistent with the gated relays of retinal activity described in other species.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited studies and comparison to other species.

claim: No distinction between TCs could be found that precluded two TCs from being innervated by the same RGC axon in normal mouse dLGN.
source: However, the most striking connectivity rule that came out of our mouse EM reconstruction was that we could find no distinction between TCs (morphology, convergence, ultrastructure) that precluded two TCs from being innervated by the same RGC axon (Morgan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is based on citation to Morgan et al., 2016.

claim: The mechanisms exist in the mouse dLGN to generate completely segregated subcircuits.
source: The odd case of the albino island eliminates the possibility that the mixing of retinogeniculate connections observed in the normal mouse reflects an upper limit of the structural specificity of the system. The mechanisms exist in the mouse dLGN to generate completely segregated subcircuits.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the demonstration of complete segregation in the albino island.

claim: The normal network organization likely reflects an adaptive balance between receptive field refinement, space, and the benefits of integrating signals from multiple RGCs.
source: The normal network organization, therefore, likely reflects an adaptive balance between receptive field refinement, space, and the benefits of integrating signals from multiple RGCs.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of why normal dLGN organization differs from the segregated island.

claim: Molecular recognition helps keep RGC axons from similar regions of the dLGN bundled together as they travel through the optic tract.
source: Molecular recognition helps keep RGC axons from similar regions of the dLGN bundled together as they travel through the optic tract (Sitko et al., 2018; Bruce et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on axon guidance.

claim: Homotypic membrane recognition molecules are required for RGC boutons to cluster together to form synaptic glomeruli.
source: Homotypic membrane recognition molecules are also required for RGC boutons to cluster together to form synaptic glomeruli (Monavarfeshani et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Monavarfeshani et al., 2018.

claim: A set of mistargeted RGC axons of the same type might be expected to stay bundled together in the absence of activity-dependent cues.
source: A set of mistargeted RGC axons of the same type might, therefore, be expected to stay bundled together in the absence of activity-dependent cues.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited molecular mechanisms.

claim: There is extensive evidence showing that developmental patterns of retinal activity are critical for shaping the architecture of retinogeniculate connections.
source: On the other hand, there is extensive evidence showing that developmental patterns of retinal activity are critical for shaping the architecture of retinogeniculate connections (Liang and Chen, 2020 for review).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: The waves of activity that propagate through the retina prior to eye opening are particularly important for eye-specific segregation and topographic refinement.
source: The waves of activity that propagate through the retina prior to eye opening are particularly important for eye-specific segregation (Feller, 2009) and topographic refinement (Grubb et al., 2003; Pfeiffenberger et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on retinal waves.
